extracted.intended_audience: federal agency officials, attorneys, legislators, and members of the public concerned with access to agency records
extracted.subtask_description: Senate floor text and debate amending section 3 of the Administrative Procedure Act (1946) to require agency publication, indexing, and public access to opinions, orders, rules, and records, and to define specific exemptions and judicial remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication in the Federal Register (section 3(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Except to the extent involved in national security secrecy or matters solely internal to agency management, every agency shall separately state and currently publish in the Federal Register for the guidance of the public: (A) descriptions of central and field organization and where/methods the public may secure information or obtain decisions; (B) statements of the general course and method by which its functions are channeled and determined, including procedures, rules of procedure, forms and instructions; (C) substantive rules of general applicability and statements of general policy or interpretations of general applicability; and (D) every amendment, revision or repeal of the foregoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication obligation is central: absent publication (or incorporation by reference), no person shall be required to resort to or be bound by matters required to be published. Exceptions limited to (1) national security/foreign policy secrecy and (2) matters solely internal to agency management. During debate Senator Humphrey suggested removing the requirement that private parties have "actual notice" prior to commencement of proceedings; Senator Long defended retaining that protection for private parties. The statute's A–D list sets the scope of what must be published and updated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of agency opinions, orders, rules, and policy interpretations (section 3(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Except where specifically required to be secret for national defense/foreign policy, related solely to internal personnel rules/practices, or specifically exempted by statute, every agency shall make available for public inspection and copying all final opinions (including concurring and dissenting), all orders made in adjudication of cases, and rules/statements of policy/interpretations that affect the public and are not required to be published in the Federal Register, unless promptly published and copies offered for sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may delete identifying details to prevent a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy or to protect the public interest, but any deletion must be fully explained in writing. Agencies must maintain and make available a current index identifying each final order, opinion, rule, policy statement, and interpretation. No final order or opinion may be cited as precedent, and no post-effective-date opinion/rule/policy may be relied on by an agency against a private party unless it has been indexed and made available or published, or private parties had actual notice of its terms prior to commencement of a proceeding. Debate shows tension between openness and protecting parties from surprise; the "prior to commencement" protection was retained to avoid binding private parties on unindexed materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency records — general availability and prompt production (section 3(c) intro)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every agency shall, in accordance with published rules stating time, place, and procedure, make all its records promptly available to any person except for specified categories of records or parts thereof that are exempted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must publish their procedures for requests; promptness is mandated. The statute then enumerates discrete exemptions (see entries below). Debate highlights concern about how broadly exemptions (especially investigatory files and confidential information) will be interpreted and the trade-offs for enforcement and data collection (e.g., wage surveys).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption — national security / foreign policy (section 3(c)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Records specifically required by Executive order to be kept secret for the protection of national defense or foreign policy are exempt from disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a categorical exemption tied to Executive orders. It mirrors traditional FOIA national security protections; agencies should identify such records under established classification rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption — internal personnel rules and practices (section 3(c)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Records that relate solely to the internal personnel rules and practices of any agency are exempt from disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects routine internal administrative matters; does not shield substantive policy or actions affecting the public. Agencies must distinguish between internal-only rules and those that affect external parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption — statutory exemptions (section 3(c)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Records specifically exempted from disclosure by statute are exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If another statute explicitly exempts certain records from disclosure, that exemption controls. Agencies must identify and cite the statutory basis when asserting this exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption — trade secrets and confidential information obtained from the public (section 3(c)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secrets and other information obtained from the public and customarily privileged or confidential are exempt from disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protection safeguards commercially or privately sensitive submissions, including trade secrets. During debate Senator Humphrey proposed adding the phrase "in confidence" to protect wage data collected by agencies (e.g., Bureau of Labor Statistics), arguing that without explicit confidentiality assurances data collection could be jeopardized; Senator Long argued the existing language ('obtained from the public and customarily privileged or confidential') was sufficiently broad and that adding 'in confidence' might encourage agencies to claim confidentiality more broadly. Agencies asserting this exemption should assess customary confidentiality practices and potential impacts on data collection essential for government functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption — intra-agency or interagency memoranda or letters on law or policy (section 3(c)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Intra-agency or interagency memoranda or letters dealing solely with matters of law or policy are exempt from disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protects deliberative communications about law or policy. Senator Humphrey had proposed extending the exemption to memoranda dealing with 'matters of fact' (e.g., credibility evaluations or factual summaries), arguing disclosure could chill candid internal judgments; Senator Long opposed broadening the exemption, warning it would lessen information available to the public. The statute as enacted limits the exemption to law or policy, so factual summaries that are otherwise publicly available are not shielded by this clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption — personnel, medical, and similar privacy-sensitive files (section 3(c)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Personnel files, medical files, and similar matters the disclosure of which would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy are exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires a privacy-balancing judgment: only disclosures constituting a 'clearly unwarranted invasion' are exempt. Agencies should apply a concrete privacy test and may delete identifying details when making opinions/orders/rules available (see section 3(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption — investigatory files compiled for law enforcement purposes (section 3(c)(7))
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigatory files compiled for law enforcement purposes are exempt except to the extent they are by law available to a private party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senator Humphrey warned that an overly broad disclosure of investigatory files (as originally drafted) could exceed court requirements (e.g., the Jencks rule) and chill witness cooperation; he proposed a more protective rule for witness statements until called to testify. Senator Long and the committee substituted the narrower language in the enacted bill to protect investigatory files from 'fishing expeditions' while allowing disclosure where law already grants access to private parties. The legislative history cites ABA committee opposition to opening investigation files generally. Agencies must reconcile law enforcement needs with any legal rights of parties to specific investigatory materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption — examination, operating, or condition reports for financial institution supervision (section 3(c)(8))
rubrics_metrics.description: Records contained in or related to examination, operating, or condition reports prepared by, on behalf of, or for the use of any agency responsible for regulation or supervision of financial institutions are exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects sensitive supervisory reports about financial institutions to preserve regulatory effectiveness and market stability. Agencies supervising financial institutions should treat such reports as exempt unless another law provides access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial remedies, de novo review, and fee/expediting provisions (section 3(c) enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon complaint, the district court where the complainant resides or where the agency is situated has jurisdiction to enjoin the agency from withholding and order production of improperly withheld records; the court shall determine the matter de novo, the burden is on the agency to sustain its action by a preponderance of the evidence, and the court may assess costs and reasonable attorneys' fees against the agency and punish noncompliance by contempt. Such proceedings shall be given precedence on the docket and expedited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute provides robust judicial review and a financial remedy incentive for compliance (attorneys' fees and costs). 'De novo' review and agency burden of proof strengthen requesters' position. Agencies should be prepared to justify withholding decisions in court on a preponderance standard. Courts are directed to prioritize these cases for expedited handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency record of votes in multi-member agencies (section 3(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Every agency having more than one member shall keep a record of the final votes of each member in every agency proceeding and, except to protect national defense or foreign policy, such records shall be available for public inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures transparency of collective decision-making in multi-member bodies (e.g., commissions). Only narrow national security/foreign policy exceptions permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on withholding authority; no withholding from Congress (section 3(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in this section authorizes withholding of information or limiting availability of records to the public except as specifically stated in this section, nor does this section authorize withholding information from Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits agency discretion to withhold information to the enumerated exemptions only and preserves congressional access. Agencies cannot use this statute as a blanket authority to withhold records beyond the listed exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'private party' (section 3(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Private party' means any party other than an agency for purposes of the section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies who benefits from certain protections and access rules; used, for example, in the investigatory-files exception and indexing/citation provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date (section 3(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: The amendment shall become effective one year following the date of enactment of this Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a one-year implementation period for agencies to publish rules, establish indexing systems, and adjust procedures to comply.
